extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate, genteel public interested in morals, manners, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical moral and social essays (The Spectator) that observe everyday behaviour, illustrate with classical allusion and comic examples, and offer prescriptive judgments about character, manners, love, and servitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy as a common, fallible art
rubrics_metrics.description: People naturally form judgments of strangers' characters from the features and lineaments of their faces; thus every one in some degree is a 'physiognomist' without formal training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that this is a natural tendency but a fallible 'art': the essay stresses that the 'air' of the face (overall expression) is generally more expressive than individual features, and that physiognomic rules (e.g., matching human features to animals) are speculative and can be overcharged. Examples/anti-patterns: the physiognomist who misjudged Socrates; authors who publish charts matching faces to animals are to be treated skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the air of the face to isolated features
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall 'air' or general expression of the face is more revealing of disposition than the mere lines or individual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming character impressions, focus on the whole countenance rather than literal resemblance to particular traits; avoid over-interpreting single tokens (e.g., a scar or crooked feature). The essay contrasts 'air' vs 'lines' and gives the injunction that air is 'nothing else but the inward Disposition of the Mind made visible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against prejudging by looks (moral injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an irreparable injustice to form fixed prejudices about people's worth from their outward appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: withhold harsh moral judgments based solely on looks (example: pitying a sour-faced man's wife, or mistaking a proud face for ill-nature). The Socrates anecdote shows that natural inclination suggested by looks can be conquered by education and virtue; cultivation of the mind trumps first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue in an ugly body merits double praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue lodged in a body that appears prepared for vice is especially admirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral worth, give additional credit to those whose behaviour contradicts a repellent or coarse appearance. The essay elevates 'amiable Piece[s] of Deformity' where cheerfulness and virtue outshine physical charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions visibly affect countenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every passion gives a particular cast to the countenance and is apt to disclose itself in some feature (eyes, eyebrows, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations of expression as natural clues to feeling (e.g., an eye cursing, an eyebrow calling a man scoundrel), but combine these with caution (do not take them as definitive proof of character). Examples used: lovers' silent languishing; eyes/eyebrows as expressive tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward animal-resemblance physiognomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The system that maps human faces to animals (ox, sheep, lion, hog) and infers corresponding mental traits is speculative and can be exaggerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat printed plates and overcharged likenesses skeptically; the essay notes the antiquity of this idea (Aristotle) but implies it should not be uncritically accepted. Historical example: courtiers telling Prince of Condé his face resembled an eagle and him taking that as praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pride and diffidence about personal appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Both excessive pride and excessive diffidence about one's person are faults arising from ignorance of one's true worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage self-knowledge: neither presume undue advantages from beauty nor be unduly depressed by defects. Practical advice: cultivate the mind and the lasting 'beauties' of character rather than fixating on natural looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social evaluation of 'beauties' (behavioural criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: People of exceptional personal beauty tend to be untractable: they expect allowances and give little to others, producing social irritations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging social compatibility or preference, prefer cheerful 'ugly' companions to proud beauties; the essay uses anecdote and letters (Rosalinda, 'Idols') to show how beauty can disrupt business, study, and civility (coffee-house idol worship, lovers neglecting duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coquetry and 'demurrage' in courtship is folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Women who indefinitely delay decisions in courtship ('Demurrers') waste their time and harm suitors and public welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against prolonged demurring: consider the shortness of life, the much shorter term of beauty, and the danger of late passion—advice is that modest refusal is proper, but persistent delay beyond reason is blameworthy; demur only 'out of Form' and as decency requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, letters, and examples to correct manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral instruction in these papers proceeds by satire, fictional letters, and advertisements that expose follies to public view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique guidance for producing such essays: illustrate points with witty letters (e.g., complaints about servants or idols), printed 'advertisements' parodying critics, and classical authority to persuade readers while amusing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis of servant insolence and its causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The present corrupt behaviour of servants (insolence, negligence, theft) is attributed largely to the custom of giving board-wages and to servants imitating their masters' libertine manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/behavioral implications: masters' practices (board-wages, indulgence, mixing with servants in public revels) encourage servant vice; to reform servant conduct, masters must alter their economy and example. Examples: grooms spoiling horses, lacqueys conducting amour affairs in masters' clothes, alehouse clamour invoking noble names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as explanatory principle for social behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependants tend to adopt the manners and vices of those they serve; social rank distinctions are weakened by such imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causes of lower-class behaviour, look upward to the masters' customs and public displays; remedy requires reforming elite example and customs (avoid cultivating disorderly habits that servants will copy). Anecdotes: servants adopting titles, running into clubs, and reflecting masters' extravagances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical admonition against indulgent desire (Platonist frame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonist idea that passions, once contracted by the soul, remain and may increase, offering a metaphysical reason to restrain obscene or indulgent desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as moral leverage: invoke classical/Platonist images (Tantalus, Virgil's Æneid) to shame excessive pursuit of sensual pleasures; rhetorical device for persuasive moralizing rather than empirical claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ classical citations and poetry to strengthen moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: Support observations and admonitions with quotations from classical authors (Ovid, Virgil, Milton, Plato) and contemporary learned men to give gravity and ornament to the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: bolster a social or moral claim with admired authorities and poetic excerpts (Milton on modesty, Virgil on punishment), using them to illuminate and dramatize the essay's lessons.
